You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Analysis: I inspected the repository and ran the test suite. All current tests pass (9 suites, 49 tests). A search for "cache" or related keywords returned nothing in the src tree, indicating the codebase currently has no concept of a configurable/custom cache. The issue requests adding the ability to set a custom cache (Closes #82). Since tests pass, it means either tests haven't been updated yet to require this feature, or additional changes are needed to expose an API to accept a custom cache. To be safe, I will add minimal changes to support providing a custom cache object via options where relevant and export a helper to set/get cache in the main module without breaking existing behavior. The goal is to introduce an optional cache option that can be passed into key functions (and default to no cache or an internal default) and ensure all existing behavior remains unchanged.
Plan: 1) Inspect the project structure and the main entry points in src to identify best place(s) to accept a cache (likely where fetch and render logic live). 2) Add a small utility module (src/cache.js) that provides a default cache implementation (a simple Map-based cache) and a way to accept a custom cache object via new functions or options. 3) Update the main export(s) to accept an options parameter that can include `cache`. For minimal change, implement a getCache(options) function that returns either options.cache or the default cache, and export it so tests can pass a custom cache. 4) Run tests to ensure nothing breaks. Commands will: open files for inspection, create new cache utility file, update index.js (or main exported file) to export getCache, run tests. I expect all tests to still pass and the code to accept a custom cache via options.cache where consumers choose to use it.

git add src/index.js && git commit -m "chore: expose getCache and DefaultCache from module entry" || true

The repository's existing code does not currently reference or use a cache module — no cache-related code was found in the src tree. To fully add configurable cache behavior, I need to (1) inspect package.json and the module entry points to decide where to expose the cache utilities (likely the package's root index.js), (2) export getCache/DefaultCache from the package entry so consumers can require them, and (3) optionally wire getCache into functions that would use caching if desired. Currently only src/cache.js was added; next I should add exports at the package entry (root index.js) so consumers can access the new cache utilities. I'll inspect package.json and repository root files, then add or modify the root index.js to export these utilities. Finally I'll run tests again to verify everything still passes.
